<explanation>
Based on your review of the file tree and README, this project is an AI infrastructure security assessment tool called “AI Infra Guard.” Its purpose is to scan AI systems for security risks by matching web fingerprints and vulnerabilities using YAML rules. The tool supports both a command-line interface (CLI) and a web user interface (WEBUI), while its core engine processes various rules against target systems.

Below is an approach to create a detailed system design diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify and label the main components:
   • Command-Line Interface (CLI): Represented by the “cmd/cli” package. This is the entry point when running in CLI mode.
   • Web User Interface: Indicated by “common/websocket” which serves static files (index.html, bundle.js) to provide a web-based scan dashboard.
   • Fingerprint & Vulnerability Processing Engine:
       - Fingerprint Matching: Found in the “common/fingerprints” directory (with submodules for parsing, preloading, etc.) and the YAML definitions under “data/fingerprints.”
       - Vulnerability Matching: Handled in part by the “pkg/vulstruct” package; YAML definitions for vulnerabilities are stored under “data/vuln.”
   • Core Scanner & Runner: The “common/runner” package is responsible for scanning, executing HTTP requests, and aggregating results.
   • HTTP Client Utilities: Provided by “pkg/httpx” for performing web requests during scan operations.
   • External AI Integration: The README mentions AI analysis when using tokens (e.g. hunyuan token, deepseek token). The “pkg/openai” package (and similar integration points) are involved here.
   • Logging & Configuration: Internal modules under “internal/gologger” and “internal/options” support logging, banner display, and configuration management.
   • Data & YAML Rule Configuration: The “data” directory holds the external fingerprint and vulnerability YAML rules, which form the “knowledge base” that drives the scanner’s behavior.

2. Show Relationships and Interactions:
   • The user interacts either via the CLI (by providing flags like “-target” or “-localscan”) or via the WEBUI.
   • In both modes, the system loads rule definitions (fingerprints & vulnerabilities) from the “data” folder.
   • The scanning engine (in “common/runner”) uses utilities (in “pkg/httpx”) to send HTTP requests to target services.
   • The fingerprint processing modules validate responses using the logic in “common/fingerprints” (parsers, matchers).
   • When vulnerability checks are triggered, the “pkg/vulstruct” component processes those outcomes against vulnerability definitions.
   • If running in WEBUI mode, the web server component in “common/websocket/server.go” serves static content and might push results via websockets.
   • Optionally, if AI-based analysis is triggered, calls might be made through the AI integrations (e.g., “pkg/openai”).
   • Logging and configuration are centrally handled by the “internal” packages, making sure that runtime parameters and output are managed cleanly.

3. Highlight Important Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Modularity: Each major function (UI, fingerprint parsing, vulnerability matching, HTTP communications) is neatly separated across packages.
   • YAML-Driven Configuration: The system uses external YAML files to define fingerprints and vulnerability matching rules, which allows for easy updates to security definitions.
   • Lightweight and Efficient Design: Emphasized in the README – small binary, cross-platform support.
   • Command Design: A clear separation between input interfaces (CLI vs. WEBUI) and the scanning engine.

4. Instructions for the Diagram:
   • Create distinct sections or boxes for each of the main components listed above:
       - UI Layer: Separate boxes for CLI and Web UI.
       - Core Engine: Blocks for Fingerprint Processor, Vulnerability Matcher, and Scanner Runner.
       - Communication Modules: HTTP Client (pkg/httpx) and External AI Integration.
       - Data Source: YAML configuration repository (using “data/fingerprints” and “data/vuln”).
       - Supporting Infrastructure: Logging and Configuration modules.
   • Use directional arrows to show how data flows:
       - From the User → (CLI or Web UI) → Core Scanner.
       - From Core Scanner → HTTP Client → Target Systems.
       - From Target Responses → Fingerprint & Vulnerability Processors.
       - From Processors → Aggregate Results → UI and Logs.
       - (Optionally) From Core Engine → External AI Services.
   • Label each component clearly and consider color coding boxes by type:
       - Blue for UI components.
       - Green for core business logic.
       - Orange for utility modules (HTTP client, logging).
       - Gray for configuration/data-repository elements.
   • Include notes to mention that YAML rules provide the dynamic structure of scan logic and that the scanning engine interacts with these definitions to match AI component vulnerabilities.

5. Tailor the Diagram to the Project Type:
   • Since this is a security assessment tool with both CLI and WEB interfaces, emphasize the separation between the interface layers and the scanning engine.
   • Clearly illustrate the modular approach that allows easy extension (for instance, adding new fingerprint rules or supporting additional vulnerability databases).
   • Note the integration with external AI analysis, if the “-ai” flag is used, to be depicted as an external service component.

By breaking the system into these detailed components and explicitly showing the interactions (data flow, dependencies, and configuration input), the resulting diagram will provide a precise, accurate, and comprehensive view of the architecture underlying AI Infra Guard. This helps both in understanding the system’s structure and in identifying potential areas for further enhancement or extension.
</explanation>
